assumptions.notes: Document real sources before publishing scenarios as factual.

scenarios.label: Taiwan Strait disruption (illustrative)
scenarios.description: Illustrative shock: Taiwan leading-edge wafer and CoWoS-style packaging largely offline for 6–12 months. US fabless GPU/CPU flows stall first; memory and China fabs partially buffer. Not a forecast—assumptions for essay stress-testing only.

assumptions.notes: Pair with cited TSMC→fabless supply edges and fab pins (Tainan, Arizona, Kumamoto). Add sourced scenario impacts before treating outputs as quantitative.

scenarios.label: HBM / memory supply crunch (illustrative)
scenarios.description: Illustrative shock: high-bandwidth memory (HBM) demand outruns supply, so the SK hynix / Samsung / Micron memory makers become the binding constraint on AI accelerators rather than wafer fabrication. NVIDIA and AMD GPU output is gated by HBM allocation. Not a forecast — assumptions for essay stress-testing only.

assumptions.notes: Pair with memory_supply edges (SK hynix/Samsung/Micron → NVIDIA/AMD). HBM is co-packaged with the GPU, so memory yield and capacity cap accelerator shipments.

narrative.title: HBM / memory supply crunch — how to read the map
bullets: HBM is co-packaged with the GPU, so when memory makers can't supply enough stacks, accelerator shipments are capped no matter how many wafers the foundry turns out.
Only three firms make HBM at scale — SK hynix, Samsung and Micron — with Micron the sole US-based source, making this a near-duopoly chokepoint (SK hynix, Samsung, Micron annual filings).
Map: the three memory makers are chokepoints and their HBM → NVIDIA / AMD arcs are disrupted; NVIDIA and AMD are stressed downstream.
Illustrative knob: HBM supply at ~70% of demand — directional, not a sourced forecast.

scenarios.label: US–China export controls deepen (illustrative)
scenarios.description: Illustrative scenario: tighter US/Dutch/Japanese export controls further restrict advanced tools (EUV already blocked; DUV and service curtailed) to Chinese fabs. SMIC, YMTC and CXMT are capped at trailing nodes; Huawei's leading-edge access tightens. China accelerates domestic toolmaking. Not a forecast — assumptions for essay stress-testing only.

assumptions.notes: Pair with ASML→SMIC (DUV) and equipment edges. Models policy tightening, not a physical disruption.

narrative.title: Export controls deepen — how to read the map
bullets: Leading-edge fabs depend on EUV and advanced DUV tools from a handful of US, Dutch and Japanese vendors, so cutting tool access caps a country's leading edge without any physical disruption.
EUV has never been licensed to China; this models tighter DUV and service restrictions reaching SMIC, with YMTC and CXMT held to trailing nodes (ASML, Huawei filings).
Map: SMIC, Huawei, YMTC and CXMT are chokepoints and the ASML → SMIC DUV arc is disrupted; their fabs are stressed.
Illustrative knob: China advanced-tool access at ~40% — policy tightening, not a shortage.

scenarios.label: Korea memory disruption (illustrative)
scenarios.description: Illustrative shock: a disruption to Korea's memory cluster (Samsung + SK hynix) removes most of the world's DRAM, NAND and HBM at once. Micron in the US/Japan/Taiwan provides partial relief; China's CXMT and YMTC offer limited mature-node substitution. Not a forecast — assumptions for essay stress-testing only.

assumptions.notes: Korea concentrates a majority of global DRAM and HBM. Pair with memory_supply edges and Korean fab pins.

narrative.title: Korea memory disruption — how to read the map
bullets: Korea concentrates the majority of the world's DRAM and HBM in two firms, so a single-country shock pulls DRAM, NAND and HBM offline at once — the memory mirror of a Taiwan logic shock.
Micron (US/Japan/Taiwan) is the only comparable relief, and China's CXMT / YMTC can substitute only at trailing nodes (Samsung, SK hynix, Micron filings).
Map: Korea, Samsung and SK hynix are chokepoints, Micron is partial relief, CXMT / YMTC are limited substitution, and HBM arcs are disrupted.
Illustrative knob: Korean memory capacity at ~20% of baseline.

scenarios.label: Japan toolchain & materials shock (illustrative)
scenarios.description: Illustrative shock: disruption to Japan's specialty chemicals, photoresist and Tokyo Electron coat/develop tools slows leading-edge output everywhere at once, because every advanced fab depends on the same narrow set of Japanese inputs. Not a forecast — assumptions for essay stress-testing only.

assumptions.notes: Pair with Tokyo Electron equips edges. Japan also dominates photoresist and key wafer chemicals not yet modeled as nodes.

narrative.title: Japan toolchain & materials shock — how to read the map
bullets: Every advanced fab leans on a narrow set of Japanese inputs — photoresist, specialty chemicals and Tokyo Electron coat/develop tools — so a Japan shock slows leading-edge output everywhere at once.
Unlike a single fab outage, this hits TSMC, Samsung and Intel in parallel because they share the same upstream suppliers (Tokyo Electron integrated report).
Map: Tokyo Electron and Japan are chokepoints with TEL → TSMC / Samsung equipment arcs stressed; leading-edge fabs are stressed.
Photoresist and wafer chemicals aren't modeled as their own nodes yet — the shock is represented through the TEL toolchain.

scenarios.label: Mature-node overcapacity glut (illustrative)
scenarios.description: Illustrative scenario: a wave of new Chinese mature-node capacity, plus UMC and GlobalFoundries expansions, outpaces demand for trailing-edge chips — collapsing prices and margins on legacy nodes used in autos, industrial and consumer. Leading-edge logic and HBM are largely unaffected. Not a forecast — a margin/oversupply story for essay stress-testing.

assumptions.notes: Oversupply, not a physical shortage. Watch SMIC/UMC/GF utilization and average selling prices on legacy nodes.

narrative.title: Mature-node overcapacity glut — how to read the map
bullets: This is a margin story, not a shortage: subsidized Chinese mature-node capacity plus UMC and GlobalFoundries expansions outpace demand for the trailing-edge chips that run cars, appliances and industrial gear.
Leading-edge logic and HBM stay largely untouched; the pressure lands on legacy-node prices and utilization (SMIC, UMC, GlobalFoundries filings).
Map: UMC, GlobalFoundries and SMIC and their mature-node fabs are stressed while the leading edge stays neutral.
Illustrative knob: mature-node utilization at ~70% — watch average selling prices, not supply.

scenarios.label: US CHIPS buildout matures (illustrative)
scenarios.description: Illustrative resilience scenario: US-based capacity (TSMC Arizona, Samsung Taylor, Intel, SK hynix Indiana packaging) reaches scale and provides a partial domestic buffer for leading-edge logic and memory. Amkor remains an OSAT buffer via its cited Korea and Philippines sites — not a US fab pin in this dataset. It reduces — but does not remove — concentration risk in Taiwan and Korea. Not a forecast — assumptions for essay stress-testing only.

assumptions.notes: A relief scenario: buffered supply arcs indicate partial domestic substitution rather than disruption.

narrative.title: US CHIPS buildout matures — how to read the map
bullets: A resilience case, not a shock: TSMC Arizona, Samsung Taylor, Intel, and SK hynix's Indiana packaging reach scale and give the US a partial domestic buffer in logic and memory.
Amkor appears as a substitution buffer through its Korea and Philippines OSAT pins — packaging onshoring is slower than fab announcements and is not modeled as a US site here.
It reduces but does not remove concentration — leading-edge capacity still centers on Taiwan and Korea (TSMC, Samsung, Intel, Micron, Amkor filings).
Map: US fab pins are partial relief, Amkor is a substitution buffer, and key TSMC → fabless arcs are buffered rather than disrupted.
Illustrative knob: US leading-edge self-sufficiency at ~35%.
